newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia Airlines buys CFM engines for A319 fleet.
newsitem.headline: Croatia Airlines buys CFM engines for A319 fleet.

text.p: Croatian state-owned flag carrier Croatia Airlines said on Friday it bought 12 CFM 56 engines worth $60 million from a French-American supplier CFM International.
The engines are for its six new A319 planes, ordered from the European consortium Airbus last month.
"This purchase may be extended with engines for other (Airbus) aircraft that are under option," sales and marketing vice president Kresimir Magdic told a news conference.
In a press release the company gave the engine-type as CFM 56-5B 6/5.
"By ordering the CFM power plant, Croatia Airlines forms conditions to save considerably in its future business development," it said.
The agreement was signed in Zagreb today by CFM's sales director for Central and Eastern Europe, Jean-Pierre Vernon, and president of Croatia Airlines, Matija Katicic.
"The reasons our engines were chosen to power Croatia Airlines A319s are reliability..., low maintenance costs and a wide network for product support," Vernon said.
He said some 85 percent of all European carriers had bought CFM engines for the above reasons and hoped Croatia might also consider it for future purchases.
The deal was also seen as advantageous for the entire economy as some 50 percent of the purchase price will be offset by exports of Croatian goods.
CFM granted it one spare engine worth $5 million free of charge, he said.
"Our economy as a whole, of which Croatia Airlines is only a part, will thus find it much easier to pay for this order," said the company's Magdic.
He confirmed previous reports that gas turbine maker Tvornica Plinskih Turbina will supply turbine components and spare parts to CFM.

"The value of the deal for the Croatian side at this stage is between $15 and $20 million. But since Croatia Airlines is definitely going to buy more planes, this cooperation can be expanded into a real partnership in the future."
The company plans to swap out and expand it current nine-plane fleet with new and larger, medium- and long-range aircraft by year 2006.
Some of its Boeing 737-200s are already 15 years old and have noisy Stage Two engines, that will soon be banned in most European countries it is currently flying to.
